mcqs.question: Which closure property is NOT required of a topology?

options.D: Contains the empty set and the whole space

mcqs.explanation: A topology need only be closed under FINITE intersections — arbitrary intersections of open sets can fail to be open.

whyOthersWrong.A: Arbitrary union closure is exactly axiom 2.
whyOthersWrong.B: Finite intersection closure is exactly axiom 3.

mcqs.question: In (R, usual topology), what is ∩_{n=1}^∞ (-1/n, 1/n)?
mcqs.explanation: The infinite intersection collapses to {0}, a single point — not open in R, illustrating why the topology axioms only require finite intersection-closure.

whyOthersWrong.A: That would be the union, not the intersection, and even then not exactly this union.
whyOthersWrong.C: 0 is in every (-1/n,1/n), so the intersection is not empty.
whyOthersWrong.D: The intersection shrinks, it does not grow to all of R.

mcqs.question: If p ∈ A, must p be a limit point of A?

options.B: No — p could be an isolated point of A

mcqs.explanation: A point can belong to a set without being a limit point of it — isolated points are the standard counterexample.

whyOthersWrong.A: False in general, as the isolated-point counterexample shows.
whyOthersWrong.C: Openness of A is unrelated to whether a given member is a limit point.
whyOthersWrong.D: Even infinite sets can have isolated points.

mcqs.question: Which union of closed sets is guaranteed to be closed?

options.D: No union of closed sets is guaranteed closed

mcqs.explanation: Dual to the open-set axioms: only finite unions of closed sets are guaranteed closed (e.g. [1/n,1] union over all n gives (0,1], not closed).

whyOthersWrong.A: Arbitrary unions of closed sets can fail to be closed.
whyOthersWrong.C: Even countable unions can fail (see the explanation).
whyOthersWrong.D: Finite unions ARE guaranteed closed, by De Morgan's laws applied to the open-set axioms.

mcqs.question: Why is the cofinite topology a valid topology on an infinite set X?

options.A: Because a finite union of finite sets is finite, and a finite intersection of finite sets is finite
options.C: Because it coincides with the discrete topology
options.D: Because every subset of X is finite

mcqs.explanation: Checking the axioms via De Morgan reduces to: complements of unions/intersections of cofinite sets stay finite, since finite unions and finite sets combine to stay finite.

whyOthersWrong.B: Infiniteness of X alone doesn't establish the axioms — the argument is about finiteness of complements.
whyOthersWrong.C: The cofinite topology is generally strictly coarser than the discrete topology on an infinite set.
whyOthersWrong.D: This is false for most infinite sets (e.g. R itself is not finite).
